name: Chinese Beef with Honey Black Pepper Sauce
writer_notes: SELECTOR: Fully board-mappable, punchy peppery-sweet glaze that is distinct from teriyaki and from the honey-garlic lane. Velveting with cornstarch means cheap sirloin comes out tender, which is exactly the budget angle. Confidence: medium. | HARVEST: Published nutrition excludes rice. Source groups under Sauce / Stir Fry.
intro_html: This is the sauce that makes people stop talking mid sentence. Honey and oyster sauce for sweetness and depth, soy for salt, and enough coarse black pepper that you taste it as heat rather than seasoning. The beef gets tossed in cornstarch first, a technique called velveting, which is how cheap sirloin ends up as tender as anything at a restaurant. Each bowl carries {{cal}} calories and {{protein}} grams of protein for about ${{cost_ps}} a serving (at everyday cost).
cost_note_html: Real Omaha store prices from our weekly grocery board (2026). They still swing by store and by what is on sale.
cost_lines: Honey, 0.75 cups: ~$4.18. Buy 1 (covers this batch with some left over).
Oyster Sauce, 5.25 tbsp: ~$0.82. Buy 1 (covers about three batches).
Rice, 5.5 cups dry: ~$1.22. Pantry staple; this batch alone uses about 2 2lb bags.
Pantry seasonings (black pepper, salt): ~$0.40. From jars you keep on hand.

Batch total: about $43.11 across 14 servings, so roughly $3.08 per bowl. This counts only the amounts this batch actually uses from each package, so it is the cost of the food in the containers, not a register receipt.

True shopping cost: about $47.56 across 14 servings, roughly $3.40 per bowl. What the register trip looks like if your pantry is already stocked. Meat, produce, and packaged items are counted as the whole packages you have to buy, since you cannot grab a partial box, can, or jar. Pantry staples you already own (rice, seasonings, oils, and long-lasting sauces) are counted at only what this batch uses.

Starting with an empty pantry? Add about $12.95 one time. That is the extra cost of buying full containers of every pantry staple in this recipe instead of just the amounts used, which puts a first shopping trip near $60.51. Those containers then feed this batch and many more after it.
cost_closing_html: About ${{cost_ps}} a bowl (at everyday cost). The honey is the surprise line item on the receipt, but it is also the whole personality of the dish, so that is money well spent.
shop_smart: Velveting is free. A spoonful of cornstarch from a box you already own turns the cheapest sirloin in the case into tender beef, which means you never need to buy a better cut for a stir fry again.
Grind the black pepper yourself and grind it coarse. Pre-ground pepper dust has lost most of its oils and will not give you the heat this dish is named for.
Buy honey in the biggest jug your store sells. The price per ounce on the little bear is a bad deal, and honey never goes bad, which makes bulk the obvious call.
Oyster sauce and mirin are one-time pantry buys that last for months of cooking. A jar of oyster sauce shows up in more Chinese recipes than almost anything else on the shelf.
make_it: Weigh your empty mixing pot and write the number down for portioning later.
Slice the beef thin against the grain, then toss it with a splash of the soy sauce and the salt until every piece is lightly coated. Let it sit 15 minutes.

Whisk the honey, oyster sauce, mirin, remaining soy sauce, and a heavy amount of coarse black pepper into a cup. Taste it. It should be aggressively sweet and aggressively peppery, because the beef and rice will tone it down.
Get a large skillet ripping hot and sear the beef in batches without moving it for the first minute. Pull each batch out just short of done.
Add the sliced onion to the pan and cook 2 to 3 minutes until it softens at the edges, then add the garlic for 30 seconds.
Pour in the sauce and let it bubble hard until it thickens and turns glossy, which takes about a minute. Watch it closely, because honey sauces go from perfect to scorched fast.
Return the beef with its juices, toss to coat, and scatter the chopped peanuts over the top just before packing so they stay crunchy.
portion_html: Weigh the rice into the containers first, then set the skillet on the scale, subtract the empty weight, and divide by 14. The sauce is thick, so use a spatula to scrape every bit of it out of the pan and spread it evenly. Every bowl lands at {{cal}} calories.

steps: Slice the beef thin and toss with soy sauce and salt to season it.
Cook the rice and whisk honey, oyster sauce, mirin, soy sauce, and coarse black pepper into a sauce.
Sear the beef in batches in a very hot skillet and set aside.
Soften the onion, add garlic, then pour in the sauce and reduce until glossy.
Return the beef, toss to coat, and top with chopped peanuts.
Weigh rice and beef into 14 containers.
